Unit 6 Seminar – Part 2: K-means on real datasets (Tasks A, B and C)¶

The seminar asks for at least one of three tasks. All three are done here, because they show different sides of k-means:

Task Data What is asked
A Iris (150 flowers, 4 measurements) k-means with several k, including k = 3; compare the clusters with the species
B Wine (178 wines, 13 chemical measurements) the same, comparing the k = 3 clusters with the wine classes 1–3
C WeatherAUS (145,460 daily weather records) k = 2 to 6, shown on 2-D scatter plots

k-means uses Euclidean distance, so only numeric measurements can be used. Label columns (species, wine class) are removed before clustering and used only afterwards, to check the result.

In [1]:
import warnings
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.optimize import linear_sum_assignment
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score, adjusted_rand_score

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="KMeans is known to have a memory leak")
FIG = "6.Unit06 Task {}.png"
COLOURS = np.array(["#1f77b4", "#ff7f0e", "#2ca02c", "#d62728", "#9467bd", "#8c564b"])


def kmeans(X, k, seed=0):
    return KMeans(n_clusters=k, init="k-means++", n_init=10, random_state=seed).fit(X)


def choose_k(X, ks=range(1, 11), sample_size=None):
    """SSE (elbow) and average silhouette for each k."""
    rows = []
    for k in ks:
        m = kmeans(X, k)
        sil = np.nan
        if k > 1:
            sil = silhouette_score(X, m.labels_, sample_size=sample_size, random_state=0)
        rows.append({"k": k, "SSE": m.inertia_, "silhouette": sil})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("k")


def plot_choose_k(table, title, fname):
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.3))
    axes[0].plot(table.index, table["SSE"], "o-")
    axes[0].set_xlabel("number of clusters k")
    axes[0].set_ylabel("SSE (inertia)")
    axes[0].set_title("Elbow method")
    sil = table["silhouette"].dropna()
    axes[1].plot(sil.index, sil, "o-", color="tab:orange")
    axes[1].set_xlabel("number of clusters k")
    axes[1].set_ylabel("average silhouette")
    axes[1].set_title("Silhouette")
    for ax in axes:
        ax.axvline(3, color="grey", ls=":", lw=1)
    fig.suptitle(title, fontsize=13)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG.format(fname), dpi=130, bbox_inches="tight")
    plt.show()


def compare_with_labels(true, clusters):
    """Cross-tab clusters against the real labels, match each cluster to one label, and score the match."""
    ct = pd.crosstab(pd.Series(clusters, name="cluster"), pd.Series(true, name="true label"))
    rows, cols = linear_sum_assignment(-ct.values)            # best one-to-one cluster -> label matching
    mapping = {ct.index[r]: ct.columns[c] for r, c in zip(rows, cols)}
    accuracy = ct.values[rows, cols].sum() / ct.values.sum()
    ct.index = [f"cluster {i} -> {mapping[i]}" for i in ct.index]
    return ct, accuracy, adjusted_rand_score(true, clusters), mapping

Task C – WeatherAUS¶

print("Shape:", weather.shape)
missing = (weather.isna().mean() * 100).round(1).sort_values(ascending=False)
missing.to_frame("% missing").T

Shape: (145460, 14)
Out[13]:
Pressure9am Pressure3pm WindGustSpeed Humidity3pm Temp3pm Rainfall RainTomorrow RainToday WindSpeed3pm Humidity9am WindSpeed9am Temp9am MinTemp MaxTemp
% missing 10.4 10.3 7.1 3.1 2.5 2.2 2.2 2.2 2.1 1.8 1.2 1.2 1.0 0.9

Preparing the data¶

  • Removed columns: RainToday and RainTomorrow are Yes/No text, and Euclidean distance needs numbers. RainToday also repeats the information in Rainfall. RainTomorrow is kept aside to help interpret the clusters afterwards.
  • Missing values: rows with any missing measurement are removed. Most of the gaps are pressure readings (about 10 %) and wind gusts (7 %). About 120,000 complete days (83 %) remain, which is plenty for clustering.
  • Rainfall is extremely skewed (most days have 0 mm, a few have over 100 mm), so it is log-transformed (log(1 + mm)). This stops a handful of storms from dominating the distances.
  • Standardising: temperatures (°C), pressure (hPa), humidity (%) and wind (km/h) use different units.
In [14]:
FEATURES = [c for c in weather.columns if c not in ("RainToday", "RainTomorrow")]
complete = weather.dropna(subset=FEATURES).reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"Rows kept: {len(complete):,} of {len(weather):,} ({len(complete) / len(weather):.1%}); "
      f"removed: {len(weather) - len(complete):,}")

W = complete[FEATURES].copy()
print(f"Rainfall skewness: {W['Rainfall'].skew():.1f} before, ", end="")
W["Rainfall"] = np.log1p(W["Rainfall"])
print(f"{W['Rainfall'].skew():.1f} after log(1 + mm)")
W_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(W)

Rows kept: 120,381 of 145,460 (82.8%); removed: 25,079
Rainfall skewness: 9.7 before, 2.1 after log(1 + mm)

k = 2 to 6¶

k-means runs on all the complete days. The silhouette needs distances between every pair of points, so it is calculated on a random sample of 10,000 days.

In [15]:
table_weather = choose_k(W_scaled, ks=range(2, 7), sample_size=10_000)
models = {k: kmeans(W_scaled, k) for k in range(2, 7)}
table_weather["cluster sizes"] = [sorted(np.bincount(models[k].labels_).tolist(), reverse=True) for k in range(2, 7)]
plot_choose_k(table_weather, "Task C – WeatherAUS: k = 2 to 6", "C1 weather choosing k")

2-D scatter plots¶

There are 12 dimensions, so each k is shown in two ways: on the first two principal components (the 2-D view that keeps the most information), and on two easy-to-read measurements, maximum temperature and afternoon humidity. 3,000 random days are plotted to keep the charts readable.

In [16]:
pca_w = PCA(n_components=2).fit(W_scaled)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx = rng.choice(len(W_scaled), 3000, replace=False)
P_w = pca_w.transform(W_scaled[idx])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 5, figsize=(26, 10))
for j, k in enumerate(range(2, 7)):
    lab = models[k].labels_[idx]
    axes[0, j].scatter(P_w[:, 0], P_w[:, 1], c=COLOURS[lab], s=6, alpha=0.6)
    axes[0, j].set_title(f"k = {k} – principal components")
    axes[0, j].set_xlabel(f"PC1 ({pca_w.explained_variance_ratio_[0]:.0%})")
    axes[1, j].scatter(complete.loc[idx, "MaxTemp"], complete.loc[idx, "Humidity3pm"], c=COLOURS[lab], s=6, alpha=0.6)
    axes[1, j].set_title(f"k = {k} – max temperature vs humidity at 3 pm")
    axes[1, j].set_xlabel("MaxTemp (°C)")
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel(f"PC2 ({pca_w.explained_variance_ratio_[1]:.0%})")
axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("Humidity3pm (%)")

fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIG.format("C2 weather clusters k2-k6"), dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

What do the clusters mean?¶

Average conditions in each cluster for k = 3, plus how often it rained that day and the next day. Those two columns were not used for clustering, so they act as an independent check:

In [17]:
def describe_clusters(k):
    lab = models[k].labels_
    prof = complete.assign(cluster=lab).groupby("cluster")[FEATURES].mean()
    prof.insert(0, "days", np.bincount(lab))
    prof["% RainToday = Yes"] = complete.assign(cluster=lab).groupby("cluster")["RainToday"].apply(lambda s: (s == "Yes").mean() * 100)
    prof["% RainTomorrow = Yes"] = complete.assign(cluster=lab).groupby("cluster")["RainTomorrow"].apply(lambda s: (s == "Yes").mean() * 100)
    return prof.sort_values("% RainToday = Yes")

print(f"Overall: rain on {(complete['RainToday'] == 'Yes').mean():.0%} of days, rain the next day on {(complete['RainTomorrow'] == 'Yes').mean():.0%}")
describe_clusters(3).round(1)

Findings and conclusions for the seminar¶

Task A – Iris¶

  • Choosing k: the elbow bends at k = 3, but the silhouette is highest at k = 2 (0.68, compared with 0.55 at k = 3). Only setosa is clearly separate; versicolor and virginica overlap. The metrics alone would suggest two groups, while domain knowledge says there are three species.
  • k = 3 compared with the species: 89.3 % of flowers (134 of 150) fall in the cluster matching their species (ARI 0.73). Setosa is matched perfectly (50/50) and versicolor almost so (48/50), but 14 of the 50 virginica were grouped with versicolor. All 16 differences lie where the two species overlap (petal length around 4.5–5.1 cm).
  • Scaling made it worse here (83.3 %, ARI 0.62). All four measurements are already in centimetres, and standardising gives the weakly informative sepal width as much influence as the petal measurements. Scaling is a decision to make, not a rule to apply automatically.

Task B – Wine¶

  • Scaling is decisive here: k = 3 on raw values matches the wine classes only 70.2 % of the time (ARI 0.37), because Proline (278–1,680) dominates the distances. After standardising, 96.6 % match (ARI 0.90).
  • Choosing k: on standardised data, the silhouette peaks at k = 3 (0.285) and the elbow bends there too, so the metrics agree with the three wine classes. A silhouette of 0.285 is modest, even though the classes separate clearly on the first two principal components.
  • k = 3 compared with the wine classes: classes 1 (59/59) and 3 (48/48) are matched perfectly. Class 2 has 65 of 71 correct.
  • What the clusters describe: class 1 wines are high in alcohol, flavanoids and proline. Class 2 wines are lower in alcohol, colour intensity and proline. Class 3 wines have few flavanoids, strong colour, low hue and low OD.

Task C – WeatherAUS¶

  • Preparation:
    • The Yes/No columns were removed.
    • 25,079 incomplete days (17 %) were dropped, leaving 120,381.
    • Rainfall was log-transformed (skewness 9.7 → 2.1).
    • All 12 measurements were standardised.
  • There are no natural clusters. The silhouette is low for every k (0.23 for k = 2 and 3, about 0.16 for k = 4–6) and the SSE falls smoothly. In the scatter plots, k-means is visibly slicing one continuous cloud of days into pieces. Weather changes gradually rather than in separate types.
  • The clusters are still useful summaries. For k = 3:
Cluster Days Typical conditions Rain that day Rain next day
Hot and dry 45,845 max 30.4 °C, humidity at 3 pm 40 % 9 % 14 %
Cool, calm, high pressure 46,937 max 19.1 °C, 1,023 hPa 16 % 15 %
Wet, windy, low pressure 27,599 7.3 mm rain, gusts 53 km/h, humidity 64 % 55 % 47 %

RainTomorrow was not used for clustering, yet the wet, windy cluster has rain the next day 47 % of the time, compared with 22 % overall. That independent check shows the clusters capture real weather patterns. With k = 4, the warm days split into "mild" and "hot", and the wet cluster sharpens (rain the next day 51 %).

  • Limitations:
    • This version of the data has no location or date, so the clusters mix climates and seasons.
    • Dropping incomplete rows may remove whole weather stations, for example those without pressure sensors.
    • k-means assumes round clusters of similar size.

Overall conclusions¶

  1. When real groups exist, k-means can recover them, but only with suitable preparation: 89 % for iris on raw measurements, and 97 % for wine after scaling.
  2. When they don't exist, k-means still splits the data. Whether the result is useful depends on interpretation (the weather types) and on preprocessing choices (the customer segments in the demo).
  3. Scaling, missing values and column choice are modelling decisions. Scaling hugely improved the wine result, slightly hurt the iris result, and its absence in the demo changed the whole segmentation.
  4. Clusters need checking from several angles: known labels where they exist (accuracy, ARI); the elbow method and silhouette; and outside variables such as RainTomorrow that weren't used for clustering.

Reflection¶

These tasks connected directly to the feedback on our team project, which said our four Airbnb segments were "relatively descriptive" and needed deeper business significance and more critical evaluation. This seminar showed practical ways to do that:

  • report how well separated the clusters are (silhouette);
  • check whether the segments survive reasonable preprocessing changes;
  • test them against outside variables, as RainTomorrow was used here.

A segment should be presented with evidence that it is stable and meaningful, not only with its average values.
